title: Find the Largest Number
prompt: Given an array of numbers, return the largest one.

steps: Assume the first element is the largest so far.
Loop through the rest of the array, starting at index 1.
Whenever a bigger number appears, update your "largest so far" value.
After the loop ends, that variable holds the true maximum.
approach.example: For [3, 7, 2]: start with largest = 3. Compare 7 > 3 → update to 7. Compare 2 > 7 → no update. Final answer: 7.

walkthroughSteps: largest starts as numbers[0], giving the loop a baseline to compare against.
The loop begins at index 1, since index 0 is already accounted for.
Each iteration checks: is the current number bigger than largest?
If yes, largest is updated. If no, nothing changes.
After the final index, largest holds the maximum value in the array.
commonMistakes: Starting largest at 0 instead of numbers[0] — fails on all-negative arrays
Starting the loop at i = 0, redundantly comparing the first element to itself

title: Reverse a String
prompt: Given a string, return it reversed, without using the built-in .reverse() array method as a shortcut.

steps: Start with an empty result string.
Walk the original string backward, from the last character to the first.
Append each character to result as you go.
approach.example: For "cat": i=2 → 't', result='t'. i=1 → 'a', result='ta'. i=0 → 'c', result='tac'.

walkthroughSteps: The loop starts at str.length - 1, the index of the last character.
Each pass appends str[i] to result, then decrements i.
Because we're reading the string back-to-front, the built string comes out reversed.
The loop stops once i drops below 0, meaning every character has been visited.
commonMistakes: Starting at str.length instead of str.length - 1 — reads undefined on the first pass
Using result = str[i] + result instead of += — works, but is slower on large strings

title: Two Sum
prompt: Given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target. Assume exactly one solution exists.

steps: A brute-force check of every pair is O(n²) — too slow for large arrays.
Instead, walk the array once, using a hash map to remember numbers already seen.
For each number, compute its complement (target - number) and check if that complement is already in the map.
If it is, that's your pair. If not, add the current number to the map and keep going.
approach.example: nums=[2,7,11,15], target=9. i=0 (2): complement=7, not seen yet → store 2→0. i=1 (7): complement=2, IS in map at index 0 → return [0,1].

walkthroughSteps: seen maps a number to the index where it appeared.
Before adding the current number, its complement is checked against the map first.
That ordering matters: checking before adding prevents a number from pairing with itself.
If a match is found, the stored index and the current index are returned immediately.
commonMistakes: Adding nums[i] to the map before checking for the complement — can wrongly pair a number with itself
Using a plain object instead of a Map — works for integer keys but Map is the clearer, safer choice

title: Reverse a Linked List
prompt: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse it in place and return the new head.

steps: Walk the list once, keeping track of the previous node (starts as null).
At each node, save a reference to the next node before it gets overwritten.
Point the current node's next backward, at prev.
Advance both prev and current forward by one node.
approach.example: For 1→2→3: after all iterations the pointers flip to 1←2←3, and prev ends on node 3 — the new head.

walkthroughSteps: next is saved first because current.next is about to be overwritten — without saving it, the rest of the list would be lost.
Each iteration flips exactly one pointer to point backward.
prev and current both advance forward, one node at a time.
When current becomes null, prev is sitting on the last node visited — the new head of the reversed list.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to save next before reassigning current.next — loses the rest of the list
Returning current instead of prev — current is null at the end of the loop

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
prompt: Given a string, find the length of the longest substring that has no repeating characters.

steps: Use a sliding window with two pointers, left and right.
Expand right one character at a time, tracking each character's last-seen index in a map.
If the current character was already seen INSIDE the current window, jump left forward past that previous occurrence.
Track the longest window size seen so far.
approach.example: For "abba": right=1 window=[0,1] 'ab'. right=2 'b' repeats inside window → left jumps to 2. right=3 'a' was seen at 0, but that's outside the window (left=2) → no jump. Max length stays 2.

walkthroughSteps: lastSeen.get(char) >= left checks whether the repeat happened INSIDE the current window, not just anywhere earlier in the string.
That check is exactly what prevents left from ever moving backward.
Moving left to lastSeen.get(char) + 1 skips past the duplicate directly, instead of shrinking the window one step at a time.
maxLength is updated every iteration by comparing against the current window size, right - left + 1.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the >= left check — jumps left backward on repeats from outside the window
Recomputing the window length with a nested loop instead of tracking it with left and right directly

title: Breadth-First Traversal of a Graph
prompt: Given a graph as an adjacency list and a starting node, return the nodes in breadth-first order.

steps: BFS explores a graph level by level, using a queue instead of recursion.
Start by queueing the start node and marking it visited.
Repeatedly dequeue a node, record it, and queue any unvisited neighbors.
Mark neighbors visited the moment they're queued — not when they're dequeued — to avoid queueing the same node twice.
approach.example: Graph: A→[B,C], B→[D], C→[D]. Start at A: visit A, queue B,C. Visit B, queue D. Visit C, D already visited so skip. Visit D. Order: A, B, C, D.

walkthroughSteps: Marking a neighbor visited at queue-time, not dequeue-time, is the key detail — otherwise the same node could be queued multiple times before it's ever processed.
queue.shift() removes from the front, so nodes are processed in the order they were discovered.
That discovery order is what gives BFS its level-by-level property.
The loop ends once the queue is empty, meaning every reachable node has been visited.
commonMistakes: Marking visited only when a node is dequeued — allows duplicate entries in the queue
Using queue.pop() instead of queue.shift() — that turns it into DFS, not BFS
